title: Has anyone here actually tried an AI agent for trading?
author: Sad_Scheme_8651
selftext:
I've been experimenting with a few different approaches to automated/AI-based trading lately and I'm curious what people here have actually used.

What AI trading agents/bots have you tried, and **which one has given you the best experience so far?**

I'm particularly interested in:

* How autonomous it actually is
* Whether you can understand *why* it makes trades
* How much control you retain
* Actual performance over time
* Whether you'd trust it with meaningful capital

Would love to hear people's experiences, good or bad.

comments.author: Cool_Big2955
comments.body: iv made a trading bot from beginning was with ai but had to take out works perfekt only on rules and python - any stock you want automaticly buy and sells on top does everything for you and tweek in .env how you want the bot to behave

replies.author: Sad_Scheme_8651
replies.body:
That's actually pretty cool. I like the fact that you've built it from the ground up and kept the strategy configurable through Python and the `.env`. I've always found that part interesting because once you start building these systems yourself, you realize how much goes into execution and position management beyond just generating buy and sell signals.

I'm actually working on something along a similar problem, but taking a slightly different approach with **Treo**. Instead of users defining all the rules themselves, I'm trying to build it more as an autonomous trading agent that makes and manages the decisions itself.

It's currently live on Binance, and one thing we've focused heavily on is keeping the user's funds in their own exchange account rather than taking custody.

If you're interested, give it a try sometime and let me know what you think. I'd genuinely value feedback from someone who's actually built a trading bot themselves.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the 'can you understand why it traded' one is where most of them fall down. plenty of bots log the order but not the reason, so when one does something weird you end up reverse engineering it from a chart.

if you're testing, make it state a reason before every order and keep it on paper until you've read a few weeks of those. I built Quantradin for that stage, an agent or a written rule trades paper money against live quotes there. free, quantradin.com.

replies.author: Sad_Scheme_8651
replies.body:
This is exactly the problem I've been thinking about. A trade log telling you *what* happened isn't nearly as useful as being able to understand *why* the system made the decision in the first place.

That's actually one of the things I'm trying to build into **Treo**. It's an autonomous trading agent rather than a traditional rule based bot, and I'm working toward making the reasoning and context behind its decisions visible rather than leaving users to reverse engineer everything from a chart.

I like the paper trading approach you've taken too. It makes a lot of sense for validating the decision making before putting meaningful capital behind it.

Treo is currently live on Binance if you're interested in trying it from the other side and comparing approaches. I'd genuinely love to hear what you think, especially given that you've built something in this space yourself.

Find it at [https://treo.live](https://treo.live)

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: good luck with it. the reason has to be written before the order goes in, not after, otherwise it's just a tidy story about a trade that already happened.

comments.author: ViciousProminence
comments.body: I trust AI more for finding setups than placing trades moon keeping the final call manual makes more sense because once a bot acts alone it gets hard to know if the edge is real

replies.author: Sad_Scheme_8651
replies.body:
Yeah, I actually agree with the concern around blindly letting a bot act on its own. The hard part isn't just finding a setup, it's knowing whether the system actually has a repeatable edge and understanding why it's taking the trade.

Where I think manual approval becomes difficult though is the 24/7 nature of crypto. If AI identifies a setup at 3am, or while you're at work, you still have to be there to make the final call. And once you're manually approving every trade, you're still carrying a pretty big part of the execution and monitoring burden yourself.

That's actually the problem I was trying to solve with Treo. Instead of AI just telling you *"here's a setup"* and leaving you to execute it, Treo is designed to analyze the market, make the decision, execute it and then manage the position continuously.

The important part for me isn't asking people to blindly trust an AI either. Treo is built around being able to see what it's doing and understand why it made a decision, while your funds remain in your own exchange account.

It's still early, so I'd genuinely be interested in your take. If you're open to it, give Treo a try with a small amount and see how you feel about the difference between AI suggesting trades and an agent actually managing them. I'd much rather hear where the approach falls short than try to convince you it's perfect.

Link: [https://treo.live](https://treo.live)

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That split makes sense, and keeping the final call manual also gives you a log of what the AI suggested versus what you did, so you can check whether its picks beat a simple baseline over time. If you do move toward automation, it's worth running on paper first and keeping hard limits outside the AI. Timing matters for setups tied to news, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source of structured inputs for that.

comments.author: CODE_HEIST
comments.body:
my experience is with TrenchersAI, which i built and used in Paper before moving to Live, so this isn't an independent review. i don't have a verified long-term performance comparison to offer.



for your control question, i'd separate stopping new entries from closing existing positions. would you want a pause button to do both, or leave exits running under the original rules?

comments.author: Blotter-fyi
comments.body: I've been trying out [Agency](https://agency.trading) with a few different models and strategies, and it's pretty cool. Very new though.
